options: The first half may be a dream built out of the second
The second half is a sequel set years later
All the characters are secretly related

quiz.q: Club Silencio tells us that every sound on stage is recorded. Why does the film confess this?
options: To explain how the theatre pays its bills
To make us distrust music we have already been moved by
To warn that the projector is failing
quiz.why: The confession arrives exactly when the song has worked on us, so it turns our own feelings into part of the trick.

quiz.q: Why does the film show us the blue key long before we learn what it opens?
options: So the plot can move faster
So the audience forgets about it
So its meaning builds before we can name it
quiz.why: An unexplained object gathers weight each time it appears; the film trusts the audience to hold the question.

The blue key and the diner behind Winkie's both return in the second half.

truefalse.fix: Adam Kesher is a film director being pushed to cast a particular actress.

shortAnswers.q: What does the film refuse to explain about the woman called Rita?
shortAnswers.model: It never says who she was before the crash, or whether her story exists outside Diane's head. It keeps her a surface, so we have to build a person out of a face and a borrowed name.

shortAnswers.q: Why does the audition scene keep the camera so calm and so close?
shortAnswers.model: The stillness lets us watch Betty become someone else the moment she starts to act. Because the camera does not cut, we cannot pretend the transformation is a trick of editing.

shortAnswers.q: What is the cost of Diane's dream in the second half?
shortAnswers.model: The dream costs her the only version of her life in which she is loved, and waking leaves her with a key, a box and a debt. The film makes the cost physical before it makes it emotional.

shortAnswers.q: Why does the last shot belong to the blue-haired woman and a single word?
shortAnswers.model: After two hours of noise the film finishes with a woman we have barely met telling us to be quiet. Silence is the only explanation it is willing to give.

quiz.q: The film opens with five minutes of work and almost no speech. What does that opening establish?

The town's hostility to outsiders
Eli's power over the workers
quiz.why: We meet the man as a body in a hole before he is allowed to explain himself, and that order never quite reverses.

quiz.q: The score sounds more like a warning than a tune. What does that do to scenes that look calm?
options: It makes the dialogue harder to hear
It keeps us tense inside them
It tells us the town band is playing
quiz.why: The strings rise under polite conversation, so the audience feels the threat before any character states it.

quiz.q: Daniel calls Eli's faith a superstition. What does the film do with that claim?
options: It has no interest in religion
It proves that Daniel is right
It shows both men using belief as a tool
quiz.why: Eli sells belief to a crowd and Daniel sells land; the film keeps the two performances side by side rather than choosing.

options: Daniel Plainview

options: Daniel Plainview
Eli Sunday

quotes.note: Eli's forced confession in the bowling alley; it is the price of his life.

truefalse.s: Daniel builds a pipeline to the coast so he can send his oil out without the railways.
Eli asks Daniel to pay for his church, and Daniel later uses that debt to humiliate him.
The film opens in a mine shaft, years before the oil business begins.
Daniel is a generous employer who shares the profits with the town.
truefalse.fix: He pays as little as he can and treats the town as land to be signed.

truefalse.s: Eli heals people and asks for nothing in return.
truefalse.fix: Eli performs healings and demands money and credit for the church.

truefalse.s: The man who arrives claiming to be Daniel's brother really is his brother.
truefalse.fix: He is an impostor, and Daniel kills him once he is sure.

shortAnswers.q: What does the film refuse to explain about Daniel's past?
shortAnswers.model: It gives us one long confession in a dark room and no dates, no family and no reason for the hatred. The gap is the point: we are asked to judge a man whose history has been kept from us.

shortAnswers.q: Why is the church scene played with Daniel on the floor and Eli above him?
shortAnswers.model: The frame gives Eli every advantage of height while the dialogue gives Daniel every advantage of money. The film wants us to feel that power can be borrowed from a room and then taken back.

shortAnswers.q: What is the cost of Daniel's competition, and who pays it?
shortAnswers.model: H.W., the man who called himself Henry, Eli's dignity and finally Daniel's own company are all spent on it. The film counts the cost in people rather than in dollars.

shortAnswers.q: Why does the last scene stay in a wide, calm frame while the violence happens?
shortAnswers.model: The stillness refuses to let the audience call the killing a thrill. By not moving, the camera behaves like a witness who has seen this before.

quiz.q: The narrator often tells us the outcome before the scene is played. What does that do to suspense?
options: It replaces suspense with judgement: we watch how, not whether
It removes all interest from the duels
It proves the narrator was in the room
quiz.why: Knowing the ending turns each scene into evidence, and the voice quietly tells us how to weigh it.

quiz.q: Why does Kubrick slowly pull the camera back instead of cutting closer in emotional scenes?
options: The lens could not focus any closer
It makes the people look small inside their own lives
It hides the actors' faces from the audience
quiz.why: Distance turns feeling into a picture, so we observe the characters instead of dissolving into them.

quiz.q: The film is lit almost entirely by candlelight. What does that do to the faces?
options: It hides which character is speaking
It makes everyone look younger
It makes them look like paintings we study rather than people we identify with
quiz.why: The soft, painted light frames every face like a portrait, which keeps us at a cool, judging distance.

truefalse.s: Barry marries Lady Lyndon after her husband dies, and her son never accepts him.
Barry escapes the army by taking another officer's uniform and papers.
Bryan, Barry's young son, dies after a fall from a horse.
Barry wins the last duel and returns to England in triumph.
truefalse.fix: He is wounded in the duel and leaves England ruined.

truefalse.s: Lady Lyndon has no money of her own and marries Barry for love.
truefalse.fix: She is very rich, and the film leaves her feelings for Barry in doubt.

truefalse.s: Barry stays a soldier for the whole film and never returns to civilian life.
truefalse.fix: He leaves the army, lives by gambling and cards, and ends in poverty.

shortAnswers.q: Why does the film keep Barry's own thoughts out of the narration?
shortAnswers.model: A narrator who judged him from inside would make him either a hero or a villain. By staying outside, the film makes Barry a surface that other people read, which is exactly what he does to them.

shortAnswers.q: What is the cost of Barry's social climbing, and who pays it?
shortAnswers.model: Bryan's death and Lady Lyndon's grief are the bills, and Barry pays with his leg and his name. The film lets the family pay first.

shortAnswers.q: Why is the last duel shot at a distance and without music?
shortAnswers.model: The wide shot makes two men look like a formality being carried out rather than a climax. With no music to tell us how to feel, we supply the judgement ourselves.

shortAnswers.q: What does the film refuse to explain about Lady Lyndon?
shortAnswers.model: It never tells us whether she loves Barry, tolerates him or is simply trapped. Her face in the candlelight is the only evidence, and it is not enough to settle the question.

options: It makes the rooms huge and the people small and strange
It makes the palace look cheap
It hides which character is speaking
quiz.why: The distorted width turns a palace into a space where people are specimens, and the darkness keeps half of each face unreadable.

quiz.q: Why does a court of 1708 speak in modern slang and swearing?
options: Because the writers could not find period sources
So the cruelty sounds like something we might say today
To show that the queen was uneducated
quiz.why: The modern idiom removes the safety of distance: these insults could be said in a corridor now.

quiz.q: Why does the last shot hold on the two women for so long?
options: It shows that Abigail has been forgiven
It is simply waiting for the credits
It leaves the question of who has won uncomfortably open
quiz.why: The film ends on a hand and a face rather than a verdict, so the audience has to decide what the victory is worth.

truefalse.s: Abigail marries Samuel Masham and gains a title and a place at court.

The battle scenes are distant, muddy and confusing rather than heroic.

truefalse.fix: She has lost seventeen children, and the rabbits stand for them.

shortAnswers.q: What is the cost of Abigail's success, and who pays it?
shortAnswers.model: She wins the queen's ear and loses any life of her own, and the last shot makes that price visible. Sarah pays too, but she keeps the one thing Abigail traded away.

shortAnswers.q: Why does the film keep the war off screen and its violence brief?
shortAnswers.model: The war is a bargaining chip in the corridors, so the film shows it as noise and mud rather than as heroism. What matters is who can end it, not who fights it.

shortAnswers.q: What does the film refuse to explain about Anne's grief?
shortAnswers.model: It never gives Anne a scene of mourning; we count rabbits instead of hearing her speak. That refusal makes the court's politeness look like a way of not saying the obvious.

shortAnswers.q: Why is the final shot so uncomfortable to watch?
shortAnswers.model: The camera stays on two faces long after the dialogue has stopped, so we cannot pretend the story is over. It asks us to watch a relationship that has turned into a job.

options: It makes the words easier to follow

It shows that the characters are ill
quiz.why: Whispering forces close attention and turns public scenes into conspiracies we are eavesdropping on.

quiz.q: Why does the film show the murder of Macduff's family rather than report it?
options: It gives Lady Macbeth more screen time
It explains the prophecy
It makes the cost of Macbeth's rule concrete
quiz.why: A reported murder is information; a shown one is a debt the audience carries into the final battle.

shortAnswers.q: What does the film refuse to explain about the witches?
shortAnswers.model: It never says whether they cause the future or only describe it, and it keeps them half out of frame. That uncertainty is what makes Macbeth's choices feel like his own.

shortAnswers.q: Why is the sleepwalking scene shot in near darkness?
shortAnswers.model: The darkness makes her hands the only bright thing in the frame, which is where the guilt is. It also stops us reading her face, so the voice has to do the work.

shortAnswers.q: What is the cost of Macbeth's ambition, and who pays it?
shortAnswers.model: His wife, his friend, Macduff's family and finally his own name are the price. The film counts the cost in bodies rather than in crowns.

shortAnswers.q: Why does the film keep the blood on faces and hands instead of washing it away?
shortAnswers.model: The blood is the only record of what has been done in a film that cuts most of the explaining. Keeping it visible makes the murders cumulative rather than separate.

quiz.q: Why does the camera keep moving in a film that is nearly all talk?
options: It shows off the office furniture
It keeps the pressure physical while the words do the damage
It hides the actors' faces
quiz.why: The restless camera turns talking into action, so a scene of men on telephones feels like a fight.

quiz.q: Blake's speech was written for the film and not for the play. What does that suggest?
options: The play had no salesmen in it
The writer had forgotten his own play
The film wants a visible outside force to start the fear
quiz.why: Blake arrives from somewhere above the office, delivers the threat and leaves, so the pressure has a face rather than a rumour.

truefalse.s: Blake appears only at the start of the film and never comes back.
Moss proposes breaking into the office to steal the leads.
Almost every outdoor scene in the film takes place at night or in the rain.
Roma is the office manager who controls the leads and the keys.
truefalse.fix: Williamson is the manager; Roma is the salesman who has to beg him.

shortAnswers.q: What does the film refuse to show us, and why does that make the office feel like a trap?
shortAnswers.model: We never see the land or the buyers, only voices and paper, so the product becomes pure talk. A trap is exactly right for men who cannot check whether anything they say is true.

shortAnswers.q: What is the cost of 'always be closing', and who pays it?
shortAnswers.model: The men pay with their sleep, their dignity and finally their jobs. The buyers pay too, in money for land that exists only on a map.

shortAnswers.q: Why is Blake's speech shot with him moving around the room?
shortAnswers.model: He invades the space of every man he speaks to, so the camera makes the threat physical without a blow. The movement also means nobody can politely look away.

shortAnswers.q: Is Shelley a victim, a thief, or both?
shortAnswers.model: He was made by this system and then discarded by it, and he steals because the system taught him that only winning counts. The film lets him be both, which is why the ending is cruel rather than satisfying.

quiz.q: The film stops to explain its jargon straight to camera, then jokes about explaining it. What does that do?
options: It lets us laugh at our own confusion while still learning the term
It proves the terms cannot be explained
It hides the plot from the audience
quiz.why: The joke admits that the subject is designed to be boring, and the explanation makes sure we cannot hide behind that excuse.

quiz.q: Why does the film cut from a bathtub to a blackjack table to a stripper with five mortgages?
options: To advertise the casinos
To make a dull system feel like a scam we can enjoy watching
To show that all the characters are friends
quiz.why: The comedy keeps us entertained by the very behaviour we are being asked to condemn.

quiz.q: Why does the film end with statistics about jobs and homes lost?
options: To prove the numbers were invented
To set up a sequel about banks
To turn the investors' win into a public cost
quiz.why: The final captions take the profit away from the characters and hand the bill to people who never appear on screen.

quotes.quote: You bet against the American economy.
options: Mark Baum
Ben Rickert
Jared Vennett
quotes.note: Said to men who have just become rich, and the film's moral centre in one sentence; a close paraphrase.

options: Michael Burry
Ben Rickert
Mark Baum
quotes.note: Baum's conclusion in Florida, and the word the film keeps returning to; paraphrased.

truefalse.s: Burry reads the mortgage documents and realises the rates will reset and many borrowers will fail.
The film uses famous faces and direct address to camera to explain financial terms.
Burry's investors try to take their money back when his bet looks wrong.
The banks refuse to sell Burry the swaps because they know the market is unsafe.
truefalse.fix: They sell gladly, because they think he is throwing his money away.

truefalse.s: The film presents the crash as a natural disaster with nobody to blame.
truefalse.fix: It names the banks, the lenders and the ratings agencies as the makers of it.

truefalse.s: Baum makes his fortune and ends the film happy.
truefalse.fix: He ends the film sickened by what the winnings mean.

shortAnswers.q: What does the film explain twice, and what does it never explain?
shortAnswers.model: It explains the jargon twice, with jokes, so nobody can claim they did not understand. It never explains why the people who saw it coming did so little, which is the harder question.

shortAnswers.q: Why does the film keep interrupting itself with direct address?
shortAnswers.model: The subject is a system designed to be unreadable, so the film has to break its own story to be understood. The interruptions are also a joke about how easily we accept nonsense.

shortAnswers.q: What is the cost of being right early, as Burry is?
shortAnswers.model: He loses his investors' trust and years of his life while everyone tells him he is wrong. Being right early looks exactly like being wrong until the moment it does not.

shortAnswers.q: Is the film an explanation or an accusation?
shortAnswers.model: It explains enough to make the accusation legible, then uses the ending to point it at named institutions. The comedy keeps the audience in the room while the charge is read out.

quiz.q: Why is the palette grey, brown and washed out?

truefalse.s: Smiley is brought back from retirement to find the mole.
Haydon is the mole.
Smiley's wife, Ann, has been having an affair with Haydon.
Smiley is loud and impatient and shouts at his colleagues.
truefalse.fix: He is quiet and patient, and he wins by listening.

truefalse.fix: There is almost no written evidence; Smiley catches him by comparing what people say.

truefalse.s: Prideaux is shot in Hungary and dies there.

shortAnswers.q: Why does the film refuse to explain the plot twice?
shortAnswers.model: It treats the audience as another intelligence officer who can hold a file in their head. The confusion is the subject: every character is working from fragments as well.

shortAnswers.q: What is the cost of Smiley's patience?
shortAnswers.model: He wins the argument and loses his wife, his friend and any belief that the service deserves him. The film lets the victory look like the loneliest possible outcome.

shortAnswers.q: Why does the camera sit still in long takes during conversations?
shortAnswers.model: Stillness makes us watch for the small betrayals, a glance or a pause, that the dialogue is hiding. Cutting would give us the excitement the film is deliberately withholding.

shortAnswers.q: What does the film leave unsaid about Ann?
shortAnswers.model: We hear about her only from men describing their own wounds. She is the one character with no scene of her own, and that absence is how the film measures what the job costs.

quiz.q: The film repeats the same pick-up with different men. What does the repetition do?
options: It turns an atrocity into a routine, then makes the routine unbearable
It shows she is learning to drive
It fills time before the plot starts
quiz.why: By the fourth van the audience knows the ending, and the film uses that knowledge to make the ordinariness sickening.

quiz.q: Why does the camera often stay inside the van at eye level?
options: It was the only way to record the sound
It puts us in the seat beside her, close enough to feel the trap close
It hides the Scottish landscape
quiz.why: Sitting at her shoulder, we become a passenger in the scene rather than a judge watching from outside it.

quiz.q: The black room has no furniture, no horizon and almost no sound. What does that space remove?
options: The need for a script
The possibility of music
Every clue that would tell us where we are or what is real
quiz.why: With nothing to measure the space against, the audience loses the bearings that would let us explain what we are seeing.

options: The woman

truefalse.s: Many of the men in the van were not actors and did not know they were being filmed.
The woman rarely answers questions about herself, and her face stays still while the men talk.
The beach sequence is filmed from a distance, and we watch people in trouble without being taken close to them.
The woman is a human being who has lost her memory.
truefalse.fix: She is something other than human, learning what people are by watching them.

truefalse.s: The motorcyclist is a police officer trying to stop her.
truefalse.fix: He is one of her own kind, watching her and clearing up afterwards.

truefalse.s: The film explains where she comes from in a short laboratory scene.
truefalse.fix: No such scene exists; the film never explains her origin.

shortAnswers.q: What does the film refuse to explain about where she comes from?
shortAnswers.model: We never see a ship, a laboratory or a home, only a van and a black room. Without an origin she becomes pure behaviour, and the audience has to read her like an animal or a child.

shortAnswers.q: Why does the film use non-actors in the van?
shortAnswers.model: Their hesitation and ordinary faces make the encounters feel unscripted, so we cannot file them safely as fiction. That discomfort is the film's real subject.

shortAnswers.q: What is the cost of her curiosity about being human?
shortAnswers.model: She loses the protection of being nothing, and the world answers her with violence. The film treats tenderness as the most dangerous thing she learns.

shortAnswers.q: Why does the score sound like an alarm rather than a melody?
shortAnswers.model: The strings scrape and repeat, so the sound says something is being tracked rather than something is being felt. It keeps the audience in the position of the watched.

truefalse.s: The film is black and white and framed almost square.
Winslow kills a gull after Wake warns him it brings bad luck.
The two men drink heavily, and the drinking blurs what is real.
Wake lets Winslow into the lamp room whenever he asks.
truefalse.fix: Wake keeps the lamp room locked and forbids Winslow to enter.

truefalse.s: Winslow is a cheerful young man who enjoys the work.
truefalse.fix: He is sullen, secretive and increasingly violent.

truefalse.s: The film ends with a rescue boat and both men going home.
truefalse.fix: No boat comes, and the ending is a violent, unexplained image.

shortAnswers.q: What does the film refuse to explain about the lamp?
shortAnswers.model: It never says what is inside the lens or why Wake worships it, and it never lets us look for long. The refusal keeps the lamp powerful in a way an explanation would ruin.

shortAnswers.q: Why is the film in black and white?
shortAnswers.model: The grey sea and white sky put the men on the same scale as the rock, so the island looks like a fact rather than a set. Colour would give the landscape a beauty the story does not allow.

shortAnswers.q: What is the cost of Wake's authority, and who pays it?
shortAnswers.model: Winslow pays with his sanity and Wake with his life, and neither of them ever admits the debt. The authority was only ever a story about a light.

shortAnswers.q: Why does the film end on an image rather than an explanation?
shortAnswers.model: An explanation would decide which of the two men's stories was true. The image leaves both versions possible and makes the audience carry the doubt out of the cinema.

quiz.q: She talks to the camera at the moments when she is least honest with the people in the room. What does that make us?
options: Accomplices in the lie rather than judges of it
Her therapists
Complete strangers
quiz.why: We are told the truth in the aside and then watch her lie, so our silence becomes part of the performance.

quiz.q: The bank manager thinks her jokes are an offer of sex. How does the scene use that?
options: It proves she wanted the loan for sex
It shows that her performance of confidence is read as something else entirely
It shows that the bank is generous
quiz.why: For once she is not trying anything, and the misreading exposes how little control she has over what she signals.

quiz.q: The episode is twenty-seven minutes and mostly comic. Where does the sadness come through?
options: In the music
In the scenes with her father
In the pauses just before and after the jokes
quiz.why: The comedy is a timing trick, and the half-second of stillness either side of a punchline is where the grief sits.

truefalse.s: Fleabag talks directly to the camera in the middle of conversations.
At the lecture, Fleabag and Claire raise their hands and find that nobody else has.
The cafe is failing, and the loan is meant to keep it open.
Fleabag goes to the bank to borrow money for a second cafe.
truefalse.fix: She needs the loan to keep the one cafe open.

truefalse.s: Claire is the best friend who died.
truefalse.fix: Claire is her sister; Boo was the friend who died.

truefalse.s: The episode ends with the loan approved and the cafe saved.
truefalse.fix: It ends on a look to camera with nothing settled.

shortAnswers.q: What does the episode refuse to say out loud about Boo?
shortAnswers.model: Boo is named and mourned only in pieces, never in a scene where someone explains what happened. The grief leaks out through jokes, which is how the show makes it feel real.

shortAnswers.q: Why does she look at the camera exactly when she is lying?
shortAnswers.model: The camera is the only place where she can be honest about being dishonest. It makes the audience a friend and an alibi at the same time.

shortAnswers.q: What is the cost of her jokes, and who pays it?
shortAnswers.model: The jokes keep her in the room but stop anyone getting close, so she pays in loneliness and the people around her pay in confusion. The show never lets the jokes buy her anything lasting.

shortAnswers.q: Is the bank scene funnier than it is sad?
shortAnswers.model: It is funny because she cannot stop performing, and sad because the performance is the only thing she has. The scene turns when he believes it and she realises she has been read wrong.
